criteria.descriptor: Correctly explains why process-local state fails under LB routing, rolling deploys, and scale-in; accurately externalizes authoritative session state to a shared store while keeping rebuildable caches local; correctly handles same-session concurrency (locking/CAS/idempotency) and the pinned-connection nature of SSE streams (draining + checkpoint resume). Full marks require no false claims — e.g. calling sticky sessions 'stateless', asserting a live stream can migrate, or treating a rebuildable cache as authoritative state.

Addresses all four asks: failure diagnosis (routing + durability), stateless redesign with a state taxonomy and store choice, the streaming/in-flight-tool wrinkle with drain + resume, and concrete trade-offs with mitigations. Full marks require the streaming/tool-idempotency nuance and the concurrency handling, not merely 'put the transcript in Redis'.

Justifies each choice by mechanism rather than assertion — why round-robin loses state, why affinity is a poor fix, why per-session serialization is cheap here, why a live stream can't be migrated, why a rebuildable handle need not be externalized — and weighs alternatives (e.g. async job vs synchronous stream) instead of naming one tool.

Reads as an organized design review with a clear authoritative-vs-rebuildable state taxonomy and precise vocabulary (statelessness, session affinity, connection draining, optimistic concurrency/CAS, idempotency, checkpoint/resume), so a reviewer can follow the argument without inferring missing links.

expected_answer_points: Diagnoses that process-local state means a follow-up request the LB routes to a different replica loses the conversation, and that rolling deploys/crashes/scale-in destroy volatile in-memory state (no durability, no shared view).

Explains that sticky sessions / session affinity are not a real fix — they re-introduce statefulness, cause load imbalance, block autoscaler rebalancing, and still lose state when the pinned replica is drained or dies.

Externalizes the authoritative session state (transcript + agent scratchpad) to a shared low-latency store keyed by session_id (e.g. Redis, optionally write-through to a durable DB) with a load→run→persist per-request flow, making the compute tier fungible/stateless.

Distinguishes authoritative session state from rebuildable per-process caches (retriever handle, model/HTTP client, connection pools) that legitimately stay local, and frames statelessness as relocating state rather than eliminating it.

Handles concurrent same-session read-modify-write races via per-session serialization or optimistic concurrency (versioning/CAS) plus idempotency keys for retried requests, to avoid lost updates or duplicated turns/tool runs.

Recognizes an SSE stream / in-flight tool run is pinned to one replica and cannot be migrated, and handles deploys with connection draining / graceful shutdown (SIGTERM, preStop, drain timeout) plus incremental checkpointing so a dropped stream can resume/replay (Last-Event-ID) without re-executing side-effecting tools.
Names concrete trade-offs — per-request store round-trip latency, consistency vs throughput of session locking, durability vs cost, and the new failure domain — each with a specific mitigation.
common_pitfalls: Proposes sticky sessions / session affinity as the solution and calls the result stateless, missing that it imbalances load, blocks autoscaling, and still loses state when the pinned replica is drained or crashes.

Moves everything — including rebuildable caches like the retriever handle, model client, and connection pools — into the shared store, treating a cache as authoritative state and adding round-trip latency for zero durability benefit.

Ignores concurrency: assumes one request per session at a time and appends to the shared transcript with no lock, versioning, or idempotency key, allowing lost updates or duplicated turns/tool executions on client retries.

Claims externalizing state makes SSE streaming stateless or that a live stream can be moved to any replica, ignoring that the connection is pinned to one socket and needs connection draining plus checkpoint-resume.
Treats 'stateless' as an absolute goal and tries to eliminate all state, rather than relocating it to a durable/shared data tier while keeping compute replicas interchangeable.

Hand-waves the trade-offs — says 'just use Redis' without acknowledging the added per-request latency, the durability-vs-cost choice, or that the store is a new failure domain that needs HA and graceful degradation.
reference_answer:
1) Why it breaks. State lives in a process-local dict, so it is bound to one replica's memory. With N replicas behind an L7 load balancer doing round-robin/least-conn routing, a session's follow-up request usually lands on a replica that never saw the first turn — the transcript/scratchpad lookup misses and the conversation is lost. The dict is also volatile: a rolling deploy, crash, OOM, or autoscaler scale-in terminates the container and every in-flight transcript with it. There is no durability and no shared view. Sticky sessions are not the fix: pinning a session_id to a replica (cookie/consistent-hash affinity) makes each replica stateful — load skews toward hot instances, autoscaling can't rebalance, and when that replica is drained or dies its pinned sessions are still lost.

2) Stateless redesign. Separate authoritative from rebuildable state. The transcript and agent scratchpad are authoritative — externalize them to a shared low-latency store keyed by session_id: Redis for hot state, optionally write-through to a durable DB (Postgres) if losing a conversation is unacceptable. Each request becomes load(session_id) → run turn → persist, so any replica is fungible and the LB needs no affinity. The retriever handle, model/HTTP client, and connection pools are derived and rebuildable — a cache, not source of truth — so they legitimately stay per-process. The principle: statelessness doesn't eliminate state, it relocates it to a purpose-built data tier and makes the compute tier interchangeable. Concurrency: two requests for one session can race read-modify-write on the transcript; since a conversation is sequential, serialize per session (per-session lock or optimistic-concurrency version/CAS) and use an idempotency key so a client retry after a timeout doesn't append a turn twice or re-run a tool.

3) Streaming / in-flight tools. An SSE response is a live TCP connection pinned to one socket on one replica for up to 90s; you cannot transparently migrate it, so 'stateless' applies to session state, not the transport. Handle deploys with graceful shutdown / connection draining: on SIGTERM stop accepting new work and let in-flight streams finish within a drain timeout (preStop hook, PodDisruptionBudget) before the pod exits. Checkpoint incrementally — persist the partial assistant message and tool results as they're produced — so if a connection still drops the client reconnects (SSE Last-Event-ID) and resumes/replays from the last checkpoint instead of losing the turn. Side-effecting tool calls must be idempotent or recorded as a step/run so a retry doesn't double-execute; for very long agent runs, prefer an async job + status-poll/webhook pattern over holding a synchronous request.

4) Trade-offs. (a) Latency: every request now pays a store round-trip — mitigate with a co-located in-region Redis, connection pooling, compact state (a rolling token window, not full history), and a short-TTL read-through cache. (b) Consistency vs throughput: per-session serialization prevents lost updates but serializes that session — acceptable because concurrent same-session requests are rare. (c) Durability vs cost: Redis alone is volatile; pairing with a durable DB costs money and write latency — choose by how catastrophic a lost conversation is. (d) New failure domain: the store must be HA and the app should degrade gracefully if it's briefly unavailable.
